This study introduces a novel class of time-varying count data models termed Poisson Autoregressive Temporal-Varying Coefficient (PAR-TVC) models. These models extend the standard Poisson Autoregressive (PAR) framework by allowing the autoregressive coefficients to evolve over time. The proposed estimation method combines a two-step approach with a Bayesian framework. To address the nonlinearity of the posterior distribution, a Metropolis-Hastings algorithm is employed. The efficacy of the estimation procedure is validated through Monte Carlo simulations. Furthermore, the model's performance is evaluated using real-world data from the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) and the Shanghai Stock Exchange (SHSE). The results demonstrate that the PAR-TVC model effectively captures the temporal dynamics of count data, offering valuable insights for financial institutions and policymakers. Additionally, the model's utility is illustrated by forecasting the daily volume of IPO applications on the SHSE. Aerosols significantly impact climate, air quality, and human health, making their accurate measurement and modeling essential. While traditional methods rely on ground-based optical sensors, satellite instruments, and chemical models, these approaches are often costly, limited in spatial coverage, or lack the necessary chemical detail. This paper introduces a novel technique that leverages stellar photometry from optical surveys to derive aerosol optical depth (AOD). By utilizing a neural network trained on data from the AERONET network, we developed a method to estimate AOD from starlight. We applied this approach to the Gaia and ZTF datasets, covering the period from 2016 to 2020, to generate global AOD maps. These maps were validated against both ground-based and satellite measurements. The resulting AOD estimates exhibit a root mean square error of 0.047 and a bias of 0.001 when compared to AERONET data. Furthermore, the new AOD maps align well with those from the MODIS satellite, showing a correlation coefficient of 0.89. This study demonstrates that stellar photometry can serve as an effective, low-cost method for generating high-resolution, global AOD maps. We anticipate that this technique will be valuable for both scientific research and operational applications. The associated code is accessible at https://github.com/astropatrol/aerospatrol.

Monte Carlo methods, particularly Metropolis-Hastings algorithms, have long been the standard for sampling configurational distributions in molecular systems. However, these approaches often suffer from poor sampling efficiency due to the high autocorrelation of Markov chains, especially in systems with complex energy landscapes. In this work, we introduce a Langevin dynamics-based Monte Carlo method designed to enhance sampling efficiency. We demonstrate that this approach yields superior sampling performance compared to Metropolis-Hastings algorithms across various molecular systems. Furthermore, we show that the Langevin dynamics-based Monte Carlo method can be integrated with other Monte Carlo techniques, such as simulated annealing, to further boost sampling efficiency. Finally, we provide evidence that this method can be combined with other Monte Carlo approaches, including replica exchange Monte Carlo, to improve their sampling efficiency. These findings suggest that the Langevin dynamics-based Monte Carlo method is a versatile and powerful tool for accelerating Monte Carlo algorithms. The source code for this method is available at https://github.com/chenyong0918/LD-MC.

This study introduces a new metric for evaluating image descriptions, termed the Human Reference Utilization (HRU) score. The HRU score quantifies the extent to which an automatic description aligns with a human reference by measuring the utilization of human reference information. Unlike existing metrics, the HRU score is grounded in the concept of information utilization, which is defined by the information-theoretic measure of mutual information. We hypothesize that the HRU score will surpass current metrics in effectiveness. To test this, we conducted experiments using the Flickr30k dataset, comparing the HRU score against five standard metrics: BLEU, METEOR, CIDEr, SPICE, and BERTScore. Results indicate that the HRU score outperforms all five baseline metrics in terms of correlation with human preferences. Furthermore, we developed a neural model to generate image descriptions optimized for the HRU score and demonstrated that these descriptions achieve higher alignment with human references compared to those generated by models optimized for the five baseline metrics. These findings suggest that the HRU score is a more effective metric for assessing image descriptions than the conventional baselines. The source code for this work is available at https://github.com/Abhishek-1999/HRU.

Fitting parton distribution functions (PDFs) to experimental data is a non-linear inverse problem that requires a Bayesian approach to derive a posteriori probability distributions. This process involves two main stages: first, constructing a likelihood function from data and a prior from theoretical assumptions to form an unnormalized posterior; and second, normalizing this posterior to extract the final PDF. While the first stage is well-established, the second has historically relied on Monte Carlo integration, which is computationally expensive and difficult to scale. This paper introduces a novel method for normalizing the posterior using a deterministic integration technique called the theory framework. We demonstrate that this approach is more efficient than Monte Carlo methods and can be easily scaled to large datasets. Furthermore, we show that the theory framework can be integrated with neural networks to create a fast, differentiable, and accurate PDF fitting framework. We validate this new method by fitting the NNPDF3.1 dataset, which includes 1,000 data points, and the larger NNPDF4.0 dataset, which contains 10,000 points. The results confirm that the theory framework is both efficient and accurate, with the NNPDF4.0 fit requiring approximately 100 times fewer function evaluations than the Monte Carlo method. Additionally, we find that the theory framework is more accurate than the Monte Carlo approach, particularly in the high-$x$ region. Finally, we present a new set of PDFs, named NNPDF4.0-FW, derived using the theory framework. These results indicate that the theory framework is a powerful tool for normalizing the posterior in PDF fitting, offering significant advantages in both efficiency and accuracy. This study employs a linearized framework to model how a turbulent jet fire responds to acoustic forcing, aiming to develop a passive control strategy for mitigating combustion instabilities. The model utilizes an active flame method, which incorporates a linearized acoustic boundary condition at the nozzle exit to simulate the acoustic field. This approach is validated against a linearized Euler solver and a linearized CFD simulation of a jet fire. The resulting model serves as a computationally efficient tool for designing passive control strategies to suppress combustion instabilities. Furthermore, the model's accuracy is confirmed through a linearized CFD simulation of a jet fire subjected to acoustic forcing, demonstrating that the linearized framework effectively captures the response of a turbulent jet fire to acoustic disturbances. The model's performance is also evaluated under conditions where the acoustic field is influenced by the flame itself, revealing that the linearized framework remains valid for acoustic amplitudes up to 10% of the speed of sound. These findings indicate that the model can be applied to investigate the interaction between acoustic fields and flames in scenarios where the acoustic field is partially driven by the flame. Ultimately, this work provides a computationally efficient method for designing passive control strategies to address combustion instabilities in jet fires. The model is implemented in the open-source CFD code, OpenFOAM.

Neutron star X-ray binaries in the Milky Way are categorized into two primary groups: transient sources, which experience periodic outbursts, and quiescent sources, which remain undetected in X-rays. This study examines the recurrence periods of transient sources and explores the nature of quiescent sources within the Galactic Centre. We find that the recurrence periods of transients follow a power-law distribution with a slope of approximately 1.7, a value consistent with the distribution of accretion disk sizes. This suggests that the recurrence period is governed by the disk's size, which in turn is determined by the fallback time of the outer disk. Consequently, the recurrence period serves as a reliable indicator of the disk's size. Furthermore, we propose that the quiescent X-ray binaries in the Galactic Centre are actually transient sources with recurrence periods exceeding 10 years. This implies that the neutron stars in these systems possess fallback disks larger than 0.1 AU. These larger disks could potentially explain the high mass accretion rates observed in these systems, which are otherwise difficult to account for. Additionally, the extended disk sizes may be responsible for the low temperatures and low ionization levels detected in the disk spectra of these quiescent binaries. Finally, we suggest that the variability observed in the optical spectra of these systems originates from the fallback disks themselves. These findings offer a unified framework for understanding the properties of neutron star X-ray binaries in the Galactic Centre. This study introduces a fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) algorithm for the bipartite vertex division problem, which involves partitioning the vertices of a bipartite graph into two sets, $A$ and $B$, such that the subgraph induced by $A$ has at most $k$ edges and the subgraph induced by $B$ is $p$-colorable. We establish that this problem is NP-complete for any fixed integer $p \geq 2$ and demonstrate that the corresponding decision problem is W[1]-hard when parameterized by $k$. Furthermore, we present an FPT algorithm for the bipartite vertex division problem with respect to the combined parameters $k$ and $p$. Finally, we define a new parameter, $r$, representing the maximum degree of the graph and prove that the problem is FPT when parameterized by $k$ and $r$. Our approach relies on a kernelization technique that reduces the input graph to a smaller equivalent instance, followed by an exact algorithm applied to this kernel. The kernelization method utilizes a reduction rule based on the $r$-bounded degree parameter and a structural result concerning the size of the kernel. The exact algorithm employs a branching strategy to solve the problem on the kernel. Additionally, we introduce a novel structural result regarding the size of the kernel, which is of independent interest. This result is derived using a combination of the reduction rule and a new structural lemma. We conclude by outlining future research directions. The source code for our algorithms is available at https://github.com/AnirbanMukherjee1998/BVDFPT.

This study introduces HyperDegrade, a novel technique designed to extend the operational lifespan of CPUs by reducing their clock frequency. Unlike conventional methods that lower frequency uniformly across all cores, HyperDegrade selectively decreases the frequency of specific cores based on their current workload. This targeted approach allows for greater frequency reductions without compromising overall system performance. The method operates by dynamically adjusting the frequency of individual cores in response to workload variations, ensuring that performance remains stable even when the total system frequency is significantly lowered. To achieve this, HyperDegrade employs a lightweight, online learning algorithm that continuously monitors workload changes and optimizes core frequencies accordingly. Experimental results demonstrate that HyperDegrade can reduce CPU frequency by up to 75% while maintaining performance levels comparable to those of a system running at full speed. These findings indicate that HyperDegrade offers a viable solution for prolonging CPU longevity, particularly in scenarios where performance degradation is acceptable. Furthermore, the approach is applicable to a wide range of CPU models, including those with up to 64 cores. This study introduces a tactical multi-agent framework designed to optimize the performance of robot teams operating under constrained computational and communication resources. Furthermore, the framework's performance is compared against a baseline where agents utilize a fixed communication topology. These findings indicate that the framework significantly enhances team utility, particularly in scenarios with limited communication resources. This paper introduces a constructive approach for embedding the representation of a finite group $G$ acting on a set $X$ into the representation of its Cartesian power $G^k$ on $X^k$, where $k$ is a positive integer. The method relies on partitioning the Cartesian power $X^k$ into equivalence classes based on the Cartesian product of the orbits of $G$ on $X$. These partitions are termed Cartesian partitions, and the associated equivalence relations are called Cartesian equivalence relations. The embedding is constructed by defining a homomorphism from $G^k$ to the wreath product of $G$ and the symmetric group on the set of Cartesian equivalence classes. This homomorphism is then composed with the induced representation of $G^k$ on $X^k$ and the permutation representation of the symmetric group on the Cartesian equivalence classes. The resulting embedding is termed the Cartesian partition embedding. We demonstrate that this embedding is irreducible if and only if the Cartesian partition of $X^k$ is irreducible. Furthermore, we establish that the Cartesian partition embedding is equivalent to the embedding derived from the Cartesian product of the primitive representation of $G$ on $X$ with the representation of $G^k$ on $X^k$ induced by the diagonal embedding of $G$ into $G^k$. Finally, we provide a concrete example illustrating the Cartesian partition embedding. The constructive nature of this embedding offers a valuable tool for analyzing the irreducibility of group representations on Cartesian powers. Additionally, the concept of Cartesian partitions of Cartesian powers can be applied to other areas, such as the study of regular languages.

The detection of gravitational waves relies on laser interferometers, which function by measuring minute variations in the arm lengths of an L-shaped configuration. These variations arise from the passage of gravitational waves and manifest as phase shifts between light beams traveling along the two arms. To enhance sensitivity, the instrument's output port is typically converted into a resonant cavity known as a signal recycling cavity. This setup creates a bandpass filter that amplifies sensitivity within a specific frequency range. However, this enhancement comes at the cost of reduced sensitivity at higher frequencies, a limitation that hinders the detection of high-frequency gravitational waves. This study introduces a novel interferometer design called the sloshing-Sagnac, which integrates a Sagnac interferometer with a Fabry-Perot cavity. Unlike conventional designs, this new configuration achieves broadband sensitivity amplification without requiring a high-finesse signal recycling cavity. Consequently, the sloshing-Sagnac design offers superior high-frequency sensitivity compared to standard interferometers. We anticipate that this advancement will enable the observation of gravitational waves from binary neutron star mergers at greater distances, thereby increasing the detection rate and improving the precision of gravitational wave parameter estimation. Furthermore, this design could serve as a valuable testbed for exploring exotic physics, such as Lorentz symmetry violation. Detailed descriptions of the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer and its associated broadband sensitivity amplification mechanism are provided. This study examines the atmospheric circulation patterns of comparative terrestrial planets within simplified global circulation models (GCMs). The model incorporates a simplified topography, a simplified radiative-convective equilibrium, and a simplified representation of vertical mixing. We analyzed the circulation patterns of Earth, Mars, and Titan across a range of rotation rates, atmospheric compositions, and surface temperatures. Specifically, we observed a transition from cyclostrophic super-rotation to geostrophic turbulence as the Coriolis parameter increased. This approach provides a practical method for identifying the most suitable atmospheric parameters for terrestrial exoplanets. This study addresses the bias inherent in the line-of-sight (LOS) component of vector magnetic field data derived from inversion algorithms. Video forecasting represents a significant challenge in computer vision, with applications ranging from autonomous driving to surveillance. The rapid expansion of social media has enabled the swift dissemination of news, yet it has also facilitated the widespread circulation of false information. While deep learning methods have been effective at detecting fake news, they require extensive training data. This dependency creates a significant barrier for identifying emerging false news events, as the scarcity of labeled data hinders the creation of effective detection models. To address this challenge, we introduce MetaFNE, a meta-learning framework designed for a few-shot false news identification task. Our approach leverages a multi-task learning strategy to learn event representations from both textual and visual data, utilizing a multi-task encoder and a multi-task attention mechanism. Furthermore, we employ a meta neural process network to learn event representations from a few-shot perspective. Extensive experiments conducted on the Twitter2015 and Twitter2017 datasets demonstrate that MetaFNE outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in few-shot scenarios. The source code for MetaFNE is available at https://github.com/ChenYi0909/MetaFNE. Ultimately, this work offers a novel solution for identifying emerging false news events in a few-shot setting, which can support the development of more effective strategies to combat misinformation. This study introduces a novel framework for creating synthetic cerebral lesions in MRI images using a Progressive Adversarial Variational Auto-Encoder (PAVAE). The model operates in two stages: initially, a Variational Auto-Encoder (VAE) learns to reconstruct MRI scans, and subsequently, an Adversarial Network (GAN) refines the outputs of the VAE to generate realistic cerebral lesions. The PAVAE framework comprises three primary components: an encoder, a VAE, and a GAN. The encoder maps input images into latent vectors, which are then processed by the VAE to produce reconstructed images. Simultaneously, the GAN evaluates the realism of these reconstructed images. To validate the model's efficacy, we conducted experiments on the BraTS 2017 dataset, a collection of T1, T1c, T2, and FLAIR MRI scans. Our results demonstrate that the proposed PAVAE framework successfully generates synthetic cerebral lesions, yielding higher FID scores compared to existing methods. Furthermore, the model effectively reconstructs MRI images and produces realistic synthetic lesions, as confirmed by both quantitative metrics and qualitative analysis. These findings indicate that the framework can create synthetic MRI images with realistic cerebral lesions, offering a valuable resource for developing and testing deep learning algorithms for brain tumor segmentation. This paper introduces a unified framework for feature extraction grounded in comparative learning, designed to enhance the performance of various existing methods. The proposed approach, termed Comparative Feature Extraction (CFE), integrates a comparative learning module with a standard feature extraction module. Within this framework, the comparative learning module utilizes a set of reference samples to learn a ranking function, which is then applied to rank the target sample against the reference set. Consequently, the final feature vector for the target sample is generated by concatenating the outputs of both the feature extraction and comparative learning modules. We evaluated CFE against nine state-of-the-art feature extraction techniques across five datasets, including two face recognition datasets and three bio-metric datasets. The results demonstrate that CFE significantly outperforms all compared methods. Furthermore, we analyzed the impact of the number of reference samples on CFE's performance and observed that increasing the reference set size generally improves outcomes. Finally, we examined the influence of the ranking function's loss weight on performance, finding that a weight of 1 yields optimal results. These findings confirm that CFE is an effective, universal framework for feature extraction. The source code is available at https://github.com/ChenYong01/CFE.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly utilized to automate tasks that require structured knowledge integration, such as answering questions grounded in specific documents. However, existing methods often fail to scale effectively to lengthy texts or handle complex integration challenges. To address these limitations, we introduce ABILITY, a framework that leverages a lightweight, structured knowledge base to enhance LLMs' capabilities in integrating structured knowledge. We validate ABILITY across two distinct domains: QA over long documents and QA over knowledge graphs. Our findings indicate that ABILITY significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art approaches in both areas. Furthermore, we demonstrate that ABILITY can be applied to a wide range of LLMs, including open-source models, without requiring access to their internal parameters. This study examines biharmonic hypersurfaces within Euclidean space that possess repetitive Laplacian and bi-Laplacian operators. We establish that a biharmonic hypersurface $x:M^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{E}^{n+p}$ with a repetitive Laplacian operator must have a constant mean curvature vector. Furthermore, we demonstrate that if $M^{n}$ is a biharmonic hypersurface in $\mathbb{E}^{n+2}$ with a repetitive bi-Laplacian operator, then $M^{n}$ is either minimal or an open subset of a cylinder $S^{1}(r)\times\mathbb{R}^{n-1}$. Finally, we prove that a biharmonic hypersurface in $\mathbb{E}^{n+2}$ with a repetitive bi-Laplacian operator and constant mean curvature must be minimal. These findings extend and refine earlier results by the authors. As a consequence, we characterize biharmonic hypersurfaces in $\mathbb{E}^{n+2}$ with a repetitive bi-Laplacian operator and a specific form of the Laplacian of the mean curvature vector. Additionally, we provide a classification for biharmonic hypersurfaces in $\mathbb{E}^{n+3}$ with a repetitive bi-Laplacian operator and constant mean curvature. These results generalize and improve upon previous work by the authors. The primary tools employed are the spectral properties of the Laplacian and bi-Laplacian operators, along with the second fundamental form.

These events correspond to a series of stick-slip phenomena, which manifest as distinct peaks in the power spectrum. These findings suggest that the acoustic signature of the peeling process is governed by a concealed stick-slip mechanism. He formulated a set of axioms for such spaces and investigated their relationship with metric spaces, specifically focusing on the embedding of metric spaces into angle spaces. The findings demonstrate that the axioms defining an abstract angle space are insufficient to guarantee the existence of an associated metric. Consequently, the concept of an abstract angle space must be expanded to include a metric, resulting in a new structure termed a metric angle space. Within this framework, the two questions originally raised by Menger are resolved. Furthermore, it is shown that the class of metric angle spaces is equivalent to the class of Euclidean spaces. As a result, the notion of an abstract angle space can be fully characterized by a specific metric condition defined on Euclidean spaces. The resolution to these long-standing problems relies on a novel metric condition, referred to as the "metric angle condition," which is introduced and analyzed in detail. Point clouds, characterized by unordered sets of 3D coordinates, present significant challenges for deep learning due to their irregular structure. To address this, we introduce a novel structure called the Transformation-Unique Smoothing (TPC) structure. This structure converts point clouds into a unique, ordered 2D matrix, thereby eliminating the difficulties associated with irregular structures. We propose a new neural network architecture, the TPC-Net, which utilizes the TPC structure to process point clouds. The TPC-Net consists of two main components: a TPC structure module and a neural network module. The former transforms the point cloud into a TPC structure, while the latter processes this structure to perform tasks such as classification and regression. We define a new metric, the Transformation-Unique Smoothing (TPS) metric, to evaluate the quality of the TPC structure. Extensive experiments on three standard datasets—ModelNet40, ShapeNetPart, and SemanticKitti—demonstrate that the TPC structure outperforms existing methods, and the TPC-Net achieves state-of-the-art results in both classification and regression tasks. These findings confirm that the TPC structure is an effective approach for handling point cloud structures. The source code for this work is available at: https://github.com/ChenYi-01/TPC.

This study introduces a novel methodology for precisely tracking damage formation in self-sensing composite materials via electrical impedance tomography (EIT). The approach leverages a genetic algorithm to optimize the inversion process, enabling the exact identification of damage locations and their corresponding severity. To validate this method, a self-sensing composite was created by embedding a piezoelectric sensor into a carbon fiber-reinforced polymer (CFRP) structure. The sensor's electrical impedance was measured at 100 discrete points across the structure's surface. These data were then utilized to reconstruct the damage profile using the proposed genetic algorithm. The results demonstrate that the reconstructed damage profile aligns closely with the actual damage, confirming the effectiveness of the new approach. Furthermore, the study highlights how the inversion accuracy is influenced by the number of measurement points and the specific characteristics of the damage. Ultimately, this work offers a practical solution for accurately monitoring damage formation in self-sensing composites using EIT, which is essential for optimizing damage-tolerant designs and ensuring the safety of composite structures. We introduce a novel method for decomposing subgroups of right-angled Artin groups (RAAGs) into amalgamated free products and HNN extensions, utilizing a specific type of homomorphism termed a "division." This approach offers a fresh perspective on the classical commensurability problem for RAAGs. Furthermore, we establish that the existence of a division between two RAAGs is equivalent to the presence of a commensurability between their associated graphs of groups. As a consequence, we demonstrate that the commensurability relation for RAAGs is not a partial order. Additionally, we prove that the existence of a division between two RAAGs is decidable. Finally, we provide a concrete example of a pair of RAAGs that admit a division yet are not commensurable. These findings are significant for the study of outer automorphisms of RAAGs and their commensurability. The results presented here are derived from the work of the first author, which was completed as the doctoral thesis titled: Divisions of right-angled Artin groups. This study introduces a novel method for accelerating iterative matrix inversion, termed the Generalized Elevated Order (GEO) technique. This approach extends the previously documented Elevated Order (EO) method, which was originally designed for 2x2 matrices. The GEO method enables the inversion of larger matrices by decomposing them into smaller submatrices, thereby reducing the number of required iterations. We present a generalized algorithm for the GEO technique and provide a detailed analysis of its computational complexity. Furthermore, we introduce a hybrid algorithm that combines the GEO method with the Strassen algorithm to further enhance performance. Our complexity analysis demonstrates that the GEO method outperforms the Strassen algorithm for matrices with dimensions between 16x16 and 64x64. Additionally, we report experimental results showing that the hybrid algorithm surpasses the GEO method for matrices larger than 64x64. The proposed algorithms are implemented in CUDA, and our experiments confirm that the hybrid algorithm achieves a 2.5x speedup over the standard iterative approach for 128x128 matrices. These findings indicate that the generalized GEO method and the resulting hybrid algorithm are effective strategies for accelerating iterative matrix inversion. The source code for these algorithms is available at https://github.com/Abhishek-1999/GEO.

Contextual linear bandits represent a significant area of research with extensive literature. In this setting, an agent selects actions based on observed contextual information to maximize cumulative rewards. A primary challenge arises from the fact that the optimal action depends on the specific context, and the agent initially lacks knowledge of this relationship. To address this, the agent must explore various actions across different contexts to learn the underlying function mapping contexts to rewards. This learning process is complicated by the high dimensionality of the context space, which can be vast. Consequently, the agent requires a certain number of observations for each context to accurately estimate the reward function. In many applications, contexts are generated by a source outside the agent's control, such as a user's profile in recommendation systems or a patient's medical history in healthcare. In such scenarios, the agent cannot influence the context distribution, making it difficult to gather sufficient data for all contexts. This issue is particularly acute in distributed systems where contexts are local to individual agents and cannot be shared. For instance, in a multi-armed bandit setup with multiple agents, each agent observes its own context and selects an arm, but contexts remain local and undisclosed to other agents. This paper investigates the contextual linear bandit problem in a distributed environment where contexts are local and unshared. We introduce a novel algorithm that achieves a near-optimal regret bound of $O(d\sqrt{T\log T})$, where $d$ represents the dimension of the linear reward function and $T$ is the time horizon. This result is surprising because it matches the optimal regret bound for centralized systems, even though the agent has no access to the context distribution. Our approach relies on a new technique for learning the linear reward function without knowledge of the context distribution. We validate our algorithm through simulations and demonstrate its effectiveness in a real-world scenario involving a contextual linear bandit for ad selection in a distributed system. We investigate how dust growth influences the vertical shear instability (VSI) in the outer regions of protoplanetary disks. Our findings indicate that dust development suppresses the VSI, primarily by reducing the gas temperature and increasing the scale height of the dust component. These changes diminish the vertical shear, which in turn weakens the instability. Consequently, dust growth can hinder the rapid inward drift of pebbles, potentially extending their residence time in the outer disk and facilitating the formation of planetesimals. This mechanism offers a viable solution to the pebble drift problem, which has long challenged planet formation models. Our results suggest that dust growth and the VSI are mutually dependent processes in the outer zones of protoplanetary disks. To accurately model dust evolution and planet formation in these regions, it is essential to account for the VSI. We conclude by outlining the necessary steps to incorporate the VSI into global dust evolution simulations. This study establishes a Liouville theorem for Ricci diminutors with constant scalar curvature, a result that serves as a counterpart to the Hopf lemma. As an application, we derive a rigidity theorem for spacelike hypersurfaces with constant scalar curvature in anti-de Sitter space, demonstrating that such hypersurfaces must be totally umbilical. Furthermore, we prove a rigidity result for spacelike hypersurfaces with constant scalar curvature in de Sitter space, showing they are either totally umbilical or possess a specific geometric structure. These findings extend and refine earlier work by B. Y. Chen, S. Ma, and Y. Wang. Additionally, we confirm that the rigidity theorem for de Sitter space holds in a broader class of spacetimes. The proof of the Liouville theorem relies on a Bochner-type formula for the gradient of the scalar curvature, which is of independent interest. Finally, we provide a complete proof of the rigidity theorem for de Sitter space within a wider category of spacetimes. These results generalize and improve upon previous contributions by B. Y. Chen, S. Ma, and Y. Wang. The primary keywords associated with this research are: Liouville theorem, Bochner formula, Ricci diminutor, and rigidity theorem.

Federated learning (FL) enables the training of deep neural networks across distributed data sources without requiring data centralization. However, existing FL methods often fail to achieve optimal performance when dealing with data drawn from diverse distributions. This study introduces a novel approach called Random Stroll for Education (RSE), which leverages the concept of random walks to enhance the efficacy of FL under diverse data distributions. The core idea involves periodically selecting a subset of data from a specific source to undergo additional training, thereby creating a specialized model for that source. This model is then shared with other data sources to improve their model performance. We demonstrate that RSE outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques in scenarios involving diverse data distributions. Furthermore, we provide a theoretical analysis showing that RSE achieves a faster convergence rate than traditional FL methods. Experimental results confirm that RSE surpasses conventional FL approaches in both convergence speed and final accuracy. The source code for this work is available at https://github.com/ChenYi0909/RSE.

Semi-supervised learning (SSL) has emerged as a promising strategy to enhance the performance of deep learning models in medical image segmentation by leveraging a small set of labeled images alongside a larger collection of unlabeled ones. However, existing SSL methods often fail to fully utilize the potential of unlabeled data, resulting in suboptimal outcomes. This study introduces a straightforward consistency regularization approach designed to improve the efficacy of SSL in medical image segmentation. The proposed method employs a two-stage framework: first, a supervised model is trained on labeled data, and second, a consistency regularization technique is applied to the unlabeled data using the initial model's predictions. We conducted extensive experiments on three public datasets—ACDC, PaSCo, and MMWHS—to evaluate the effectiveness of this approach. The results demonstrate that our method outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques. Furthermore, we provide a detailed analysis of the consistency regularization process to offer insights into its underlying mechanisms. The Internet of Vehicles (IoV) represents a significant evolution in intelligent transportation systems, enabling vehicles to communicate with one another, infrastructure, and users via the Internet. This connectivity facilitates advanced applications such as autonomous driving, traffic optimization, and intelligent transportation services. However, the massive volume of data generated by IoV creates substantial challenges for storage and processing. Federated learning (FL) offers a promising solution by allowing data to remain on local devices while enabling collaborative model training across a network. Concurrently, blockchain technology provides a secure, decentralized, and tamper-proof framework ideal for supporting FL in IoV environments. This paper presents a comprehensive literature review on integrating blockchain with FL for IoV. We examine the benefits and limitations of various FL and blockchain architectures, analyze their potential applications in IoV, and discuss future research directions. The goal is to establish a solid foundation for developing a secure, efficient, and reliable blockchain-supported federated learning framework for IoV. Ultimately, this work aims to enhance the security and privacy of IoV systems. The findings are organized into four sections: an introduction, a review of FL and blockchain technologies, an analysis of their integration in IoV, and a conclusion.

Video identification systems are essential for enhancing public safety and security, yet they face significant challenges regarding energy consumption and computational complexity. While Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks have been widely adopted for video identification, their high energy usage and computational demands hinder their deployment in resource-constrained environments. This paper introduces a method and hardware co-design approach to optimize energy efficiency in LSTM-based video identification systems. First, we propose a novel energy model for LSTMs that incorporates the effects of tensor decomposition and quantization. Leveraging this model, we develop a hierarchical Tucker tensor decomposition technique to reduce the energy consumption of LSTMs. Furthermore, we introduce a quantization strategy that balances energy savings with identification accuracy. To validate our approach, we designed a hardware accelerator for the optimized LSTM architecture and implemented it on a Field-Programmable Gate Array (FPGA). Experimental results demonstrate that our optimized LSTM achieves a 99.9% identification accuracy, representing a 90% reduction in energy consumption compared to the standard LSTM. Additionally, our optimized architecture offers a 1.5x higher throughput than the conventional LSTM. These findings confirm that our method and hardware co-design effectively lower energy usage while maintaining high identification accuracy. This paper examines the decomposition of function iterates into prime components and investigates the uniqueness of such decompositions. We establish that for any finite set $X$, the iterate $f^n$ admits a unique decomposition into primes if and only if $f$ is a cyclic permutation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for any finite set $X$ and any function $f: X \to X$, the iterate $f^n$ can be decomposed into primes if and only if $n$ is a multiple of the order of the cyclic part of $f$. Finally, we prove that for any finite set $X$ and functions $f, g: X \to X$, if $f^n = g^n$ for some $n \geq 1$, then $f$ and $g$ share the same cyclic part. These results are derived using a novel approach to decomposing function iterates into primes, which we also detail. As an application, we show that for any finite set $X$ and functions $f, g: X \to X$, the equality $f^n = g^n$ implies $f^{n+1} = g^{n+1}$ for all $n \geq 1$, thereby confirming a conjecture by D. K. Dutta and S. K. Ghosh. Additionally, we provide a positive resolution to a conjecture by J. Aczel regarding the uniqueness of solutions to the equation $f^n = g^n$. Our findings rely on a new method for decomposing function iterates into primes, which is described in full. We conclude by outlining the paper's organization. The results presented herein are joint work with S. K. Ghosh.

Bayes factors serve as a valuable tool for comparing models, particularly in scenarios where p-values are unsuitable. However, their practical application has been hindered by the high computational costs associated with estimating marginal likelihoods. This paper introduces a suite of strategies designed to maximize the utility of Bayes factors while minimizing computational demands. We demonstrate that combining multiple methods yields optimal results, with the specific combination depending on the complexity of the models under consideration. To validate these strategies, we applied them to a range of models for analyzing the cosmic microwave background (CMB) and large-scale structure (LSS) data. Our findings indicate that a simple model incorporating only CMB data offers the best fit for the combined CMB and LSS dataset. Furthermore, we observed that the optimal strategy for estimating marginal likelihoods shifts as model complexity increases. These strategies are applicable to any model comparison task involving Bayesian analysis. The associated software is available at https://github.com/LSPE-Group/BF_strategies.

Discourse markers (DMs) are essential for conveying the intended meaning of text, yet they remain difficult for machines to process. While numerous studies have attempted to classify DMs into categories like additivity or temporality, these efforts have primarily relied on manual annotation. This approach is both costly and prone to subjectivity. In this work, we introduce DiscSense, a system that automatically evaluates the semantic correctness of discourse category labels for specific instances. We validate the utility of this automatic assessment by demonstrating that it aligns with human judgments. Furthermore, we show that incorporating this semantic evaluation into a neural classifier significantly enhances the accuracy of discourse category classification. To support these findings, we created a dataset comprising 10,000 instances of English DMs annotated with both discourse categories and DiscSense scores. We make this dataset and the DiscSense system publicly available at https://github.com/linguagelab/DisSense. Ultimately, we argue that this automatic semantic evaluation can serve as a valuable tool for improving discourse category classification and for assessing the quality of discourse-annotated datasets.

We examine the OPE segment between two scalar operators in AdS$_{3}$, which corresponds to a conformal block in the dual CFT$_{2}$ involving two scalar and two spinning operators. By applying a conformal transformation to the CFT$_{2}$, we convert this block into a four-point function where the two scalar operators are separated by a finite distance, while the two spinning operators reside at infinity. The results indicate that the CNN can accurately predict halo weight function data from simulations where the velocity field has been altered. Furthermore, the model demonstrates that the velocity field significantly influences the halo weight function, particularly at high halo masses. These findings suggest that the velocity field plays a crucial role in halo formation and evolution, potentially serving as a valuable probe for understanding dark matter physics. Additionally, the results imply that the halo weight function is a non-local function of the halo mass, a conclusion that aligns with the predictions of the halo finders used in the simulations. The CNN's ability to predict halo weight function data from simulations with modified velocity fields suggests that the halo weight function is a non-local function of the dark matter phase space distribution. This insight could be valuable for developing new halo finders and for utilizing halo weight function data to infer dark matter properties from observational data. Ultimately, this research highlights the importance of incorporating velocity information into dark matter halo studies. This study employs a relativistic initial principles framework to investigate the electronic structure of Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states arising from magnetic adatoms and dimers on a metallic surface. The analysis utilizes a relativistic tight-binding model to construct the surface's electronic band structure, which is subsequently folded into a reduced zone. This approach enables the determination of the electronic structure for a specific Mn adatom and two distinct configurations of Mn dimers on the Nb(110) surface. The resulting band structures reveal the formation of YSR states, which manifest as sharp peaks within the superconducting gap of Nb. These findings align with previous initial principles calculations and experimental observations. Furthermore, the study examines the influence of spin-orbit coupling and the magnetic moment on the YSR states. The results indicate that spin-orbit coupling significantly alters the band structure, whereas variations in the magnetic moment have a negligible effect. Additionally, the analysis of the local density of states (LDOS) demonstrates that the YSR states are predominantly localized around the Mn adatom and dimer sites. Finally, the study explores the impact of the Mn adatom's and dimers' magnetic moments on the supercurrent flowing between them, revealing that increasing the magnetic moment reduces the supercurrent. These results suggest that the supercurrent between the Mn adatom and dimers is highly sensitive to their magnetic moments. Overall, this work provides a relativistic initial principles framework for investigating YSR states in magnetic adatoms and dimers on metallic surfaces, offering valuable insights into the electronic structure of such systems. The proposed framework is applicable to various magnetic adatoms and dimers on metallic surfaces. Skin cancer remains a significant global health concern, with the number of diagnosed cases rising rapidly. While deep learning has shown promise in detecting skin carcinomas, its performance often degrades when encountering outlier samples. This study introduces a novel framework that leverages entropy to identify and filter these outliers, thereby enhancing the accuracy of skin carcinoma detection. We evaluated our approach using the ISIC 2018 dataset, which comprises 12,900 images across six categories: melanoma, basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, actinic keratosis, dermatofibroma, and vascular lesions. Our findings indicate that integrating entropy with deep learning significantly improves detection performance. Specifically, the framework achieved an accuracy of 98.9%, surpassing the 98.3% accuracy of a standard deep learning model. Furthermore, the proposed method reduced the F1 score for the melanoma class by 0.01 compared to the conventional approach. These results demonstrate that incorporating entropy effectively identifies outlier samples, leading to overall performance gains. The source code for this framework is available at https://github.com/AbdulrahmanAlshammari/Skin_Carcinoma_Detection.

Muon colliders represent a promising new frontier in high-energy physics, offering a unique environment for investigating electroweak symmetry breaking and exploring physics beyond the Standard Model. A defining characteristic of muon colliders is the dominance of vector boson fusion (VBF) processes at high energies, which are absent in hadron and electron colliders. This study introduces a novel Monte Carlo method designed to efficiently simulate VBF events at muon colliders. The approach combines a sector-based decomposition of the phase space with a multi-channel integration technique to ensure uniform event distribution. We validate the method's accuracy and efficiency by comparing it against the MadGraph5_aMC@NLO framework. Furthermore, we apply the algorithm to simulate VBF processes in muon colliders operating at center-of-mass energies of 3, 4, and 6 TeV. Our results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves a significant efficiency gain of approximately two orders of magnitude compared to MadGraph5_aMC@NLO. Additionally, we analyze the differential cross-sections for VBF events at these various energy levels. These findings confirm that the new algorithm is both accurate and highly efficient, making it a valuable tool for studying VBF processes at high-energy muon colliders. The source code for this method is available at https://github.com/ChenYi1999/MEFVMuon.

This paper offers a historical overview of the interplay between Godel's incompleteness theorems and Tarski's undefinability theorem, alongside the contributions of Carnap and Rosser. It examines Godel's original proof of his first incompleteness theorem, the subsequent proof by Jeroslow, and Godel's demonstration of his second incompleteness theorem. Furthermore, it details Tarski's proof of his undefinability theorem, Rosser's refinement of Godel's first theorem, and Godel's response to Rosser's extension of the second theorem. The discussion also covers Godel's and Tarski's proofs of their respective diagonalization lemmas, Rosser's proof of his theorem, and the derivation of Godel's and Tarski's diagonalization lemmas from Rosser's theorem. Finally, the paper presents Godel's and Tarski's demonstrations that their first incompleteness and undefinability theorems hold for Peano Arithmetic (PA) and Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory (ZF), respectively, when formulated using Rosser sentences rather than Godel sentences. It concludes by outlining Godel's and Tarski's proofs that their second incompleteness and undefinability theorems remain valid under the same conditions. The historical narrative is supported by relevant excerpts from the works of Godel, Tarski, Carnap, and Rosser. Readers are encouraged to consult the references for additional details on the proofs discussed. Invariant sets, such as fixed points, periodic orbits, and invariant manifolds, are fundamental to the study of dynamical systems. This paper examines invariant surfaces within a specific class of three-dimensional systems characterized by a fractional order derivative. We demonstrate that, under certain conditions, no invariant surfaces exist for these systems. Furthermore, we establish that the existence of a line of fixed points serves as a necessary condition for the presence of an invariant surface. These findings are significant for analyzing the chaotic behavior of fractional order systems. As a practical application, we prove that the Lorenz system, when its fractional order is less than 1.5, does not exhibit chaotic dynamics. Additionally, we show that the Chua system, with a fractional order of 1.5, lacks chaotic behavior. These results are derived using the Lyapunov function method. Finally, we provide a counterexample to a claim made by Li et al. (Chaos, Solitons & Fractals, 109, 108-113, 2018), which asserted that the fractional order Chua system could display chaotic dynamics when the fractional order was less than 1.5. Our analysis confirms that such systems do not possess chaotic attractors. The conclusions of this work are supported by numerical simulations. The primary keywords for this research are: Invariant surface, fractional order, dynamical system, Lyapunov function, and Chua system.

This study addresses the inverse problem of determining the boundary conditions for a structural acoustic system. The system consists of a vibrating plate coupled with an acoustic cavity, where the boundary conditions are defined by a combination of Dirichlet, Neumann, and Wentzell-Robin types. To solve this, we first establish the existence and uniqueness of solutions for both the direct and inverse problems using a fixed point argument. Subsequently, we derive a global Carleman estimate for the associated wave system. Finally, we utilize this estimate to develop a uniqueness result for the inverse problem and design an explicit algorithm to reconstruct the boundary conditions. Numerical experiments are included to validate the proposed method. The findings demonstrate that the boundary conditions can be uniquely determined from interior measurements of the acoustic pressure and the normal velocity of the plate. These results are significant for non-destructive testing and for identifying unknown boundary conditions in structural acoustic systems. The methodology relies on Carleman estimates and a uniqueness-by-determination approach, which are applicable to other structural acoustic systems with complex boundary conditions. This work extends the results in [11] by considering a more general set of boundary conditions. The paper is organized as follows: Section 2 defines the direct and inverse problems; Section 3 derives the global Carleman estimate; Section 4 proves the uniqueness of the solution for the inverse problem; Section 5 details the algorithm for reconstructing the boundary conditions; and Section 6 presents numerical examples.

We examine the dark matter (DM) phenomenology of the minimal scoto-seesaw model, the most elementary extension of the standard scoto-seesaw framework. In this variant, the dark sector comprises a singlet scalar and a singlet fermion, with the latter serving as the DM candidate. We identify the viable parameter space that satisfies all direct and indirect DM constraints, neutrino oscillation data, and electroweak precision measurements. Our analysis reveals that the singlet scalar must be light, with a mass below 100 GeV, to satisfy direct detection limits. Furthermore, we find that indirect detection constraints are most stringent for WIMP masses near 40 GeV. To address these constraints, the DM must undergo co-annihilation with the singlet scalar or a nearly degenerate heavy neutrino. We also investigate vacuum stability, demonstrating that the singlet scalar mass must exceed 100 GeV to ensure stability up to the Planck scale. Finally, we explore the phenomenology of the most fundamental model where the DM is a Dirac fermion, which requires two right-handed neutrinos. In this scenario, indirect detection constraints are significantly weaker, allowing for a broader range of DM masses. We conclude by proposing a testable signature for this model at the High-Luminosity LHC. These findings suggest that the minimal scoto-seesaw framework is a compelling candidate for the origin of neutrino masses and the nature of dark matter. The model is testable at current and future colliders, and its predictions for dark matter indirect detection are within the reach of planned experiments. Additionally, the minimal Dirac variant offers a viable framework for neutrino masses and dark matter that could be investigated at the High-Luminosity LHC. This work represents the first comprehensive study of dark matter phenomenology in the most basic scoto-seesaw models.
